summary: Defines a new IMAP special-use attribute, \Important, and a keyword, $Important, and creates an IANA registry for IMAP folder attributes. The registry includes attributes from earlier RFCs, including RFC 6154.

plainLanguage.summary: This adds a label for the folder of your most important mail, and a sticker for single messages, and keeps an official list of folder labels.

questions: what is the imap important keyword
what is the imap mailbox name attributes registry
subtitle: A message keyword and a folder attribute that let IMAP servers say 'this mail is probably important to you'.

tldr.problem: IMAP had the \Flagged flag for mail a user marks for follow-up, but no standard way for a server to signal that a message, or a whole folder, is generally important based on heuristics.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the $Important message keyword and the \Important special-use mailbox attribute, and creates an IANA registry called IMAP Mailbox Name Attributes that also lists the attributes from earlier RFCs.
tldr.outcome: Servers and clients now have shared names for importance triage that stay distinct from \Flagged, and new mailbox attributes can be registered in one place.

today: RFC 8457 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 6154.

sections.title: What the RFC Adds
sections.content:
RFC 8457 builds on two earlier IMAP documents: RFC 3501, which defines message keywords, and RFC 6154, which lets servers tag mailboxes with a special purpose through the LIST command. It adds four things.

  • A new message keyword, $Important, for messages considered important to the user by some externally defined criteria.
  • Its registration in the IMAP Keywords registry from RFC 5788.
  • A new special-use attribute, \Important, for a mailbox holding such messages.
  • A new IANA registry for IMAP mailbox attributes, filled with the new attribute and the ones from RFC 5258, RFC 3501 and RFC 6154.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail programs already had a star for things you want to follow up on. This adds a separate sticker for mail that is probably important, plus a folder label for it.

sections.title: The $Important Keyword
sections.content:
The $Important keyword signals that a message is likely important to the user. It is generally expected to be set automatically by the system, using signals such as who the message is from, who else it is addressed to, an evaluation of the subject or content, or other heuristics. A user can also set it, but that is not expected to be the main usage.

The RFC separates it from the \Flagged system flag in two ways. First, $Important means general importance, a form of triage, while \Flagged stays a mark for special attention, follow-up or time sensitivity. Messages that are like this one under the server's heuristics will also tend to be $Important. Second, $Important is based at least partly on heuristics, whereas \Flagged is only meant to be set by the user, for example with a flag or star button.
sections.plainLanguage: A star is something you put on a letter yourself. The important sticker is put there by a helpful mail clerk who guesses which letters matter to you.

sections.title: The \Important Mailbox Attribute
sections.content:
The \Important attribute marks a mailbox that contains messages likely to be important to the user. Where the server also supports $Important, the RFC says this is likely a virtual mailbox that collects messages from other mailboxes that carry the keyword. Other implementations might put messages there using the same sort of heuristics. The difference from \Flagged for mailboxes mirrors the difference for messages.

The formal syntax extends the use-attr rule from RFC 6154 using ABNF: use-attr =/ "\Important". In the RFC's examples, a LIST for Imp* returns the mailbox Important Messages with the attribute, and a CREATE with USE (\Important) succeeds on a server that advertises CREATE-SPECIAL-USE.

Two failure examples use the USEATTR response code: one where an \Important mailbox already exists, and one where the server does not support the extension. The same code is used in both cases, so only the human-readable text tells them apart, and the client cannot parse that text.
sections.plainLanguage: A folder can wear a name tag saying it is the important-mail folder. If you ask for a second one, or the server has never heard of such tags, it says no, and its note says why.

sections.title: How Servers and Clients Treat the Two Marks
sections.content:
This non-normative section describes intended usage. On the server, \Flagged is set or cleared only in response to an explicit client command. $Important is set by a heuristic process that usually looks at header fields, the mailbox the message is filed in, perhaps content and attachments. A client command can still set or clear it, and the server may use that to adjust its heuristics. A server may also decide later that a message is important, for example because the user opens it often.

On the client, \Flagged usually gets an icon such as a flag or star, with a way for the user to toggle it. $Important typically gets a lesser indication, and the client may or may not let the user change it.
sections.plainLanguage: You decide when a letter gets a star. The clerk decides about the important sticker, and listens if you say it was wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6154 apply: telling a client about special-use mailboxes exposes a small bit of extra information that could be valuable to an attacker. Identifying important messages, or the place where they are kept, could give an attacker a strategic starting point. If the algorithm that decides what is important is well known, still more is exposed, for example that certain senders are particularly significant to the mailbox owner.

As RFC 6154 notes, it is wise to protect the IMAP channel from passive eavesdropping. The RFC points to Section 11 of RFC 3501 for using the IMAP STARTTLS command.
sections.plainLanguage: If a burglar learns which drawer holds your most important letters, they know where to look first. So keep the conversation with the mail server private.

sections.title: The IANA Actions and the New Registry
sections.content:
IANA registered $Important in the IMAP Keywords registry as a PRIVATE keyword, advisory in nature, with intended usage COMMON and the IESG as change controller.

IANA also created the IMAP Mailbox Name Attributes registry, which is shared with JMAP for Mail. Entries have an attribute name (registered without the initial backslash and treated as case-insensitive), a description, a reference and free-form usage notes. Registrations in an IETF consensus document use IETF Review. Other requests go to IANA by email under Expert Review, where the expert gives only a general check that the reference and description are adequate, close to a first come first served policy.

The initial entries include All, Archive, Drafts, Flagged, Junk, Sent and Trash from RFC 6154, HasChildren, HasNoChildren, NonExistent, Remote and Subscribed from RFC 5258, Marked, NoInferiors, Noselect and Unmarked from RFC 3501, and Important from this RFC. Several of the older ones carry the usage note 'not used by JMAP'.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now one official list of folder labels, kept by IANA. Anyone with a good reason can ask to add a new label, and the list-keeper is told not to be picky.

Usually the server, by heuristics; the user may also set it

data.title: Finding the \Important mailbox
data.code:
C: t1 LIST "" "Imp*"
S: * LIST (\HasNoChildren \Important) "/" "Important Messages"
S: * LIST (\HasNoChildren) "/" "Imported Wine"
S: t1 OK Success
